questions.stem: The $x$- and $y$-components of an acceleration vector are given by the equations a$_{x}\ = (t\ -\ 6)\ \mathrm{m/s}^{2}$ and a$_{y}\ = (4\ t\ -\ 5)\ \mathrm{m/s}^{2}$, respectively, where $t$ is the time in seconds. What is the magnitude of the acceleration vector at $t = 2\ \mathrm{s}?$

The components of a velocity vector are given by the functions $v_{x}\ = (2\ t\ -\ 2)\ \mathrm{m/s}$ and $v_{y}\ = (t\ -\ 7)\ \mathrm{m/s} ,$ where $t$ is the time in seconds. What are the magnitude and direction of the velocity vector at $t = 3\ \mathrm{s}?$ Magnitude Direction
Consider two vectors, $\vec{A} =\ 3\hat{i} +\ 1\hat{j}$ and $\vec{B} =\ -1\hat{i} -\ 3\hat{j}$. Which of the following is a true statement about the vector sum $\vec{A} +\ \vec{B}$?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is a vector that has a smaller magnitude than both $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$, but nonzero.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is a vector that has a greater magnitude than both $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is a vector of length zero.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is a vector that has the same magnitude as both $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$.

questions.stem: $\vec{A}$, $\vec{B}$, $\vec{C}$, and $\vec{D}$ are vectors which have equal magnitudes but point in different directions, as shown in the figure. Which of the following resultant vectors has the greatest magnitude?

Vectors $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$ lie in the $xy$-plane with the angle $\phi$ referenced to the positive $y$-axis and the angle $\theta$ referenced to the positive $x$-axis, as shown in the figure. Which of the following is the resultant vector of $\vec{A} +\ \vec{B}$ in unit vector notation?

An object moves in the $xy$-plane a distance A at an angle $\theta$ measured counterclockwise from the positive $x-$ direction, where $0\ <\ \theta\ <\ 90^{\circ}.$ The object then moves a distance $B$ in the positive $x$-direction. The change in the $x$-component of the object's position is equal to the change in the $y$-component of its position. What is $B$ in terms of A and $\theta$? A
Vectors $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$ are drawn with the magnitudes and directions shown. Which of the following best represents the vector $\vec{B} -\ \vec{A}$?

An object is moving with an initial velocity $\vec{v}_{1}\ = (3.00\hat{i} +\ 4.00\hat{j})\ \mathrm{m/s}$ . After a certain time interval, its velocity is $\vec{v}_{2}\ = (-8.00\hat{i} +\ 15.0\hat{j})\ \mathrm{m/s}.$ What is the magnitude of the change in velocity of the object over this time interval?

In relation to a school, a student's house is located at a distance $B$ away and at an angle $\theta$ from the $x$-axis in the coordinate system shown in the figure. Starting from the school, the student takes a bus and travels a distance A in the positive $x$-direction, and then gets off the bus. What is the position vector $\vec{r}$ of the student's house relative to where the student gets off the bus?

The position of an object moving along the $x$-axis is described by $x(t) =\ 5\ t^{2}\ -\ t^{3}$ where $x$ is in meters and $t$ is time in seconds. What is the average velocity of the object during the time interval from $t$ = 1 s to $t = 3\ \mathrm{s}?$

The position-time graph shown represents the motion of a car moving along a straight road during the time interval $t$ = 0 to $t\ =\ 6\ \mathrm{s}$. Consider the instantaneous speed at two different times as $v_{1}$ at $t$ = 1 s and $v_{5}$ at $t\ =\ 5\ \mathrm{s}$ and the average speed $v_{avg}$ over the entire time interval. Which of the following is the correct ranking of these three speeds?

\includegraphics[width=0.37\linewidth]{media/u1_12_q1_9.png}

The position of an object moving along the $x$-axis is given by the equation $x(t) =\ t^{2}\ -\ 6\ t\ +$ 9, where $x$ is in meters and $t$ is time in seconds. Does the object's direction of motion change and what reasoning supports that claim?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No, because $x\ \geq\ 0$ at any given time.

choices.label: B
choices.text: No, because the acceleration is constant and nonzero.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Yes, because the object is located at the origin at $t = 3\ \mathrm{s}.$

choices.label: D
choices.text: Yes, because the velocity of the object changes sign at $t = 3\ \mathrm{s}.$

questions.stem: The graph represents the position $x$ of an object as a function of time $t$. Compare the directions of the velocities $v_{A}$ and $v_{B}$, and the directions of the accelerations a$_{A}$ and a$_{B}$, of the object at times $t_{A}$ and $t_{B}$. Velocities Accelerations

An object's position as a function of time is modeled by the equation $x\ =\ 0.5\ t^{3}\ +$ 2 where $x$ is in meters and $t$ is in seconds. What is the acceleration of the object at $t = 3\ \mathrm{s}?$
A cart's position as a function of time is $x\ =\ 10\ t^{3/2}\ +\ t$, where $x$ is in centimeters and $t$ is time in seconds. What is the cart's velocity at $t = 4\ \mathrm{s}?$

Two objects, Object $1$ and Object $2,$ have velocities $\vec{v}_{1}\ = (3\ t^{2}\hat{i} +\ 5\ t\hat{j})\ \mathrm{m/s}$ and $\vec{v}_{2}\ = (5\ t^{2}\hat{i} -\ 3\ t\hat{j})\ \mathrm{m/s} ,$ respectively, where $t$ is time in seconds. Which of the following correctly indicates the relationship between the magnitudes of the acceleration a$_{1}$ of Object $1$ at $t\ =\ 1\ \mathrm{s}$ and the acceleration a$_{2}$ of Object $2$ at $t = 1\ \mathrm{s}?$

An object moves in one dimension along the $x$-axis. At time $t\ =\ 0,$ the object is located at position $x = 1\ \mathrm{m}$ and has a velocity $v\ =\ 1\ \mathrm{m/s}.$ The object's acceleration varies as a$= 3\ t$, where a is in m/s$2$ and $t$ is time in seconds. A student incorrectly derives the equation for the object's position as $x\ =\ t^{3}/2\ +$ 1, where $x$ is in meters. Which of the following describes a possible error that could have resulted in the incorrect equation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The student's equation does not account for the initial position of the object.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The student's equation does not account for the initial velocity of the object.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The student's equation does not substitute a$= 3\ t$ in the at$2/2 term.$

choices.label: D
choices.text: The student's equation should not have a $+1$ term, as integrating the acceleration function twice yields $x\ =\ t^{3}/2.$

questions.stem: Students testing two different toy cars on a straight track determine that, starting from rest, Car A reaches a velocity $v_{A}$ in a displacement of $x_{A}$ and Car B reaches a velocity of $2\ v_{A}$ in a displacement of $2\ x_{A}$ . The motion of each car can be modeled with constant acceleration. If the acceleration of Car A is a$_{A}$, what is the acceleration of Car B?

A graph of velocity $v$ as a function of time $t$ for the one-dimensional motion of an object is shown. The object has an initial position $x_{0}=0.$ Which of the following statements best justifies whether the object will return to position $x\ =\ 0$ during the time interval $0\ <\ t\ \leq$ 3 s?

\includegraphics[width=0.29\linewidth]{media/u1_13_q1_10.png}

choices.label: A
choices.text: No, because the distance between the object and its initial position is increasing during the entire time interval.

choices.label: B
choices.text: No, because the object has a constant acceleration during this time interval.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Yes, because the velocity of the object is zero at $t = 3\ \mathrm{s}.$

choices.label: D
choices.text: Yes, because the acceleration of the object is negative during this time interval.

questions.stem: On a distant planet where the acceleration due to gravity is $\mathrm{g}_{P}$, an object takes a time $t_{P}$ to reach the ground when dropped from a height $\mathrm{h}_{0}$. On a small moon of the planet, the acceleration due to gravity is $\mathrm{g}_{P}/16.$ How long does it take an object to reach the ground when it is dropped from the same height on the moon?
At time $t\ =\ 0$ an object is thrown vertically upward. It then returns to its initial position at $t\ =\ t_{f}$. What is the speed of the object at $t\ =\ 2\ t_{f}/3?$
A car traveling in a straight line slows down at a constant rate and comes to a stop as it travels a distance $\Delta x$ in time $t$. What was the car's initial velocity?

A car is initially at rest and driven along a straight road with a constant acceleration a. The car has a velocity $v$ when it has traveled a distance $d$. A second car starts from rest on the same road and has an acceleration $3$a until it reaches the same final velocity. How far does the second car travel?

A car travelling at an unknown initial speed in a straight line is described by the time $(t)$ and position $(x)$ data shown in the table. Which of the following claims about the signs of the car's velocity and acceleration is correct, and how does the data provide evidence for the claim?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The car has a positive initial velocity and a negative acceleration because the position values are positive and are decreasing.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The car has a positive initial velocity and a negative acceleration because the position is decreasing and the magnitude of displacement in each time interval increases.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The car has a negative initial velocity and a negative acceleration because the position values are positive and are decreasing.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The car has a negative initial velocity and a negative acceleration because the position is decreasing and the magnitude of displacement in each time interval increases. \includegraphics[width=0.35\linewidth]{media/u1_13_q7_11.png}

questions.stem: An object moves in one dimension along the $x$-axis as described by the position versus time graph shown in the figure. During the time interval of the graph, how many times does the object change direction and what feature or features of the graph justifies this response?

choices.label: A
choices.text: One time because the graph indicates that there is a single point where the object's velocity is zero and its acceleration is zero.

choices.label: B
choices.text: One time because the graph indicates that there is a single point where the object's velocity is zero and its acceleration is nonzero.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Two times because the graph indicates that the velocity of the object is zero at two different points.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Two times because the graph indicates that the position of the object is zero at two different points.

questions.stem: The graph of velocity $v$ as a function of time $t$ for one-dimensional motion of an object is shown. Which of the following statements about the position of the object at $t\ =\ 8\ \mathrm{s}$ is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The position of the object is $4\ \mathrm{m}$ , because the object moves from $-$2m to $+2\ \mathrm{m}$ during the entire time interval.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The position of the object is $4\ \mathrm{m}$, because the area under the velocity graph is $4\ \mathrm{m}$ during the time interval when $v$ is positive.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The position of the object is the same as its position at $t\ =\ 0,$ because the velocity is zero exactly halfway through the time interval.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The position of the object is the same as its position at $t\ =\ 0,$ because the area under the velocity graph is zero for the entire time interval. \includegraphics[width=0.32\linewidth]{media/u1_13_q9_12.png}

questions.stem: A cart traveling along a straight track accelerates from an initial velocity of $6\ \mathrm{m/s}.$ The graph shows the cart's acceleration a as a function of time $t$. What is the displacement of the cart in meters as a function of $t$?

A bus is moving forward at $5\ \mathrm{m/s}$ when a student on the bus tosses an apple upward and toward the front of the bus. With respect to the moving bus, the apple has an initial velocity of $10\ \mathrm{m/s}$ at an angle of $60^{\circ}$ above horizontal. Which of the following correctly describes the magnitude $v_{0}$ and angle $\theta_{0}$ of the apple's initial velocity relative to an observer standing on the ground?
Car A is traveling east with a speed of $30\ \mathrm{m/s}.$ Car B is traveling north with speed of $40\ \mathrm{m/s}.$ What is the direction of the velocity of Car B relative to Car A?

A student seated in a slowly moving bus holds a ball out at arm's length and releases it. Immediately afterward, the driver of the bus applies the brakes, causing the bus to slow at a rate of $4\ \mathrm{m/s}^{2}$. Which of the following is closest to the vertical component of the acceleration of the ball while the bus slows down as seen by the student?

A toy plane which maintains an airspeed $v_{P}$ flies between points A and B in a time $t_{0}$ when there is negligible wind. When the air is moving at a velocity of $v_{P}/2$ from Point B to Point A, the toy plane can make the trip from A to B in $t_{AB}$, and the return trip from B to A in $t_{BA}$. How do the three travel times compare?

The position-time graph represents the motion of two cars, Car S and Car T, moving in the same, straight path. At which of the indicated times, $t_{1}$, $t_{2}$, $t_{3}$, and $t_{4}$, would Car S first appear to be moving in the negative direction as observed by a passenger in Car T?

A boat is traveling across a river with a current, as shown in the figure. The boat has a speed $v_{B}\ =\ 4\ \mathrm{m/s}$ relative to the water, and the current has a speed $v_{C}\ =\ 3\ \mathrm{m/s}$ relative to the shore. What is the velocity of the boat relative to the shore?

Three cars traveling on a straight two-lane road are located at the positions shown in the figure. The speeds and directions of the cars $1,\ 2,$ and $3$ relative to the ground are $v_{1}\ =\ 20\ \mathrm{m/s}$ to the east, $v_{2}\ =\ 25\ \mathrm{m/s}$ to the east, and $v_{3}\ =\ 15\ \mathrm{m/s}$ to the west, respectively. The relative velocity of Car $2$ with respect to Car $1$ is $v_{21}$, the relative velocity of Car $3$ with respect to Car $2$ is $v_{32}$, and the relative velocity of Car $3$ with respect to Car 1 is $v_{31}$. Which of the following correctly ranks the magnitudes of the relative velocities?

An observer standing on the ground measures the speed of a train as $v_{T}\ =\ 18\ \mathrm{m/s}$ to the right. Relative to the observer, a stone is launched upward and to the left with a speed $v_{S}\ =\ 10\ \mathrm{m/s}$ at an angle $\theta\ =\ 45^{\circ}$ from the horizontal, as shown in the figure. What is the speed at which the stone was launched relative to the train?

An airplane flies horizontally at a constant velocity $v_{0}$ relative to the ground over a stationary observer. The plane releases one package when it is located a horizontal distance $D$ to the left of the observer, and then releases a second package when it is located a horizontal distance $D$ to the right of the observer, as shown in the figure. The observer measures the first package to have a speed of $v_{1}$ when released, and the second package to have a speed of $v_{2}$ when released. Which of the following statements correctly compares $v_{1}$ and $v_{2}$?

questions.topic_title: Motion in Two or Three Dimensions
questions.stem: An object starts at rest and then moves in the $xy$-plane with the components of acceleration a$_{x}$ and a$_{y}$ each varying as represented by the acceleration-time graph shown. At what time or times during the time interval shown is $(are)$ the magnitude of the acceleration at a maximum, and what reasoning supports this claim?

choices.label: A
choices.text: At $t\ =\ t_{f}/2.$ The product a$_{x}$a$_{y}$ is at its greatest value.

choices.label: B
choices.text: At $t\ =\ t_{f}/2.$a$_{x}$ and a$_{y}$ are equal in magnitude.

choices.label: C
choices.text: At $t$ = 0 and $t\ =\ t_{f}$. $|$a$_{x}\ -$ a$_{y}|$ is at its greatest value.

questions.stem: Object $1$ is launched at an initial speed $v_{0}$ at an angle $\theta$ above the horizontal and reaches a maximum height of $y_{1}$. Object $2$ is launched at an initial speed $2\ v_{0}$ at the same angle $\theta$, reaching a maximum height of $y_{2}$. What is the relationship between $y_{1}$ and $y_{2}$?

questions.topic_title: Motion in Two or Three Dimensions
questions.stem: Two boats cross a river that has a current of velocity $v_{r}$, as shown. The boats have identical speeds with respect to the water. Boat $1$ heads at an angle upstream such that it reaches the opposite shore directly across from its starting point. Boat $2$ heads in a direction perpendicular to the current and reaches a position on the opposite shore downstream of its starting point. Which boat takes less time to cross the river, and what reasoning supports this claim?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Boat $1$ takes less time because it travels a shorter distance than Boat $2.$

choices.label: B
choices.text: Boat $1$ takes less time because its velocity with respect to the water and the current velocity add together, giving Boat $1$ a greater resultant velocity.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Boat $2$ takes less time because its velocity has a greater $y$-component with respect to the ground than Boat 1.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Boat $2$ takes less time because the current increases the boat's speed relative to the ground. \includegraphics[width=0.36\linewidth]{media/u1_15_q4_18.png}

questions.topic_title: Motion in Two or Three Dimensions
questions.stem: A projectile is launched from level ground at an initial velocity $v_{0}$ and angle $\theta$ as shown in the figure. At the instant the projectile is moving horizontally, it hits a wall and then bounces directly back at half the speed it had just before impact. Assuming the projectile is in contact with the wall for a negligible time, which of the following expressions represents the total time the projectile is in the air from leaving ground level to reaching ground level again?

questions.topic_title: Motion in Two or Three Dimensions
questions.stem: Two identical balls, Ball $1$ and Ball $2,$ are hit from the same initial position and move along the trajectories shown in the figure. The initial speed of Ball $1$ is less than that of Ball $2.$ Which ball takes less time to return to the ground, and what evidence supports this claim?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ball $1$ takes less time. Its initial speed is less than that of Ball $2.$

choices.label: B
choices.text: Ball $1$ takes less time. The horizontal distance it travels is less than that of Ball $2.$

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ball $2$ takes less time. Its initial speed is greater than that of Ball $1.$

choices.label: D
choices.text: Ball $2$ takes less time. The maximum height it reaches is less than that of Ball $1.$

If both the speed and the angle with which the projectile was launched were doubled, what would the new speed be when it lands?

questions.stem:
An object is launched at time $t\ =\ 0$ from a height $H$ above the ground with an initial velocity $v_{0}$ at an angle $\theta_{0}$ below the horizontal, as shown in the figure. With respect to the indicated coordinate system, which of the following is a correct expression of the position vector $\vec{r}$ as a function of $t$ for the object after it is launched?

choices.label: D
choices.text: $\vec{r} = (-\frac{1}{2}\ gt^{2}\ +\ v^{0 t cos \theta 0})\hat{i}+(H\ -\ v^{0 t sin \theta 0}\ -\ \frac{1}{2}\ gt^{2})\hat{j}$

questions.topic_title: Motion in Two or Three Dimensions
questions.stem: On Earth, an object is launched horizontally with an initial speed $v$ at a height $\mathrm{h}$ and lands at a horizontal distance $x_{E}$ from its launch point. An astronaut on the surface of the Moon horizontally launches an object with the same initial speed $v$ and height $\mathrm{h}$, and this object lands at a horizontal distance $x_{M}$ from its launch point. What is the ratio $x_{E}/x_{M}$ in terms of the acceleration of gravity $\mathrm{g}_{E}$ near Earth's surface and $\mathrm{g}_{M}$ near the Moon's surface?

A $24\ \mathrm{cm}$ long rectangular bar is composed of two uniform $12\ \mathrm{cm}$ bars of different materials, A and B, with the same cross-sectional area as shown. The density of material B is twice the density of material A. The long bar is cut through its center of mass and perpendicular to its long axis. What is the ratio of the mass of the left piece to the mass of the right piece?

A bar with a non-uniform density is launched from the ground with an initial center-of-mass speed $v_{0}$ at an angle $\theta$ above the horizontal and lands at the same level from which it is launched as shown. The distance $d$ is measured from right end of the bar when it is launched to the left end of the bar when it lands. During flight, the object experiences some rotation about its center of mass. Which of the following initial and final orientations of the bar's center of mass $x_{\mathrm{cm}}$ would maximize $d$?

Six identical uniform spheres are arranged on a set of coordinate axes in two different triangular arrangements, A and B, as shown. How does the $y$-coordinate of the center of mass of the three spheres in arrangement A, $y_{\mathrm{cm},A}$ compare to the $y$-coordinate of the center of mass of the three spheres in arrangement B, $y_{\mathrm{cm},B}$?

choices.label: D
choices.text: Cannot be determined without knowing the coordinates of the vertices of each triangle \includegraphics[width=0.42\linewidth]{media/u2_21_q3_26.png}

questions.stem: A system consisting of three identical uniform bars is placed in four different locations on the $xy$-plane as shown. At which of the four locations is the system's center of mass located farthest from the origin $O$?

A $0.50\ \mathrm{m}$ long rod lies along the $+x$-axis with one end of the rod at the origin. The rod's linear density is $\lambda\ =$ A $-\ Bx$ where A $=\ 2.0\ \mathrm{kg}/\mathrm{m}$ and $B\ =\ 1.0\ \mathrm{kg}/\mathrm{m}^{2}$. What is the $x$-position of the center of mass of the rod?

A uniform sheet of cardboard is cut into an ``L'' shape as shown. One end of string is attached at point P, and the object is held vertically at rest by the string. Which of the following diagrams best represents this rest position as the shape is supported by the string?

Three small, uniform objects, A, B, and C, are arranged as shown with each object's center of mass a distance $\mathrm{L}$ from the origin. Objects A and B each have the same mass, $M$, and are at positions $45^{\circ}$ above and below the $-x$-axis, respectively. The center of mass of the three-mass system is at the origin. Which of the following relationships describes Object C's mass $\mathrm{m}_{C}$?

The center of mass of an irregularly shaped platform is balanced on a pivot Point P with coordinates $(7.0\ \mathrm{m}$, $1.0\ \mathrm{m}).$ Two rocks are then placed on top of the platform, as shown in the top view. One rock has a mass of $1.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ and is located at $(-$2.0 m, $-3.0\ \mathrm{m}),$ and the second rock has a mass of $3.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ and is located at $(5.0\ \mathrm{m}$, $4.0\ \mathrm{m}).$ At which coordinates should a third rock of mass $4.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ be placed such that the three rock-platform system is balanced?

A system consists of three uniform spheres connected by a uniform rod passing through the center of each sphere. The rod has a length of $2.0\ \mathrm{m}$ and mass of $1.0\ \mathrm{kg}$, and the spheres have a mass of $1.0\ \mathrm{kg}$, $3.0\ \mathrm{kg}$, and $2.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ located in positions as shown. What is the distance between the center of the $3.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ sphere and the center of mass of the system?

A block is at rest on a desk's horizontal surface. A student correctly identifies the forces exerted on the block as the force of Earth on the block and the force of the desk on the block. A book then is placed between the block and the desk. Which objects exert forces of equal magnitude on the block after the book has been introduced?

choices.label: D
choices.text: Earth, the book, and the desk

questions.stem: At the instant shown in the figure, a string attached to a box on an inclined surface is pulling straight up on the box. There is negligible friction between the box and the surface. Which of the following free-body diagrams best indicates the direction of the forces exerted on the box at the instant shown in the figure?

Two blocks, A and B, are attached together with a string and pulled up an incline by another string attached to Block B, as shown. The string between the blocks has a tension $F_{T}$ and the other string attached to Block B has a tension $F_{P}$. There is negligible friction between the surface and the blocks. The free-body diagram of Block B is shown. Which of the following correctly identifies the force labeled $F_{1}$ in the free-body diagram and provides the correct justification?

choices.label: A
choices.text: $F_{1}\ =\ F_{P}$ because Block B is pulling the string down the incline.

choices.label: B
choices.text: $F_{1}\ =\ F_{P}$ because the string attached only to Block B is also pulling Block A up the incline.

choices.label: C
choices.text: $F_{1}\ =\ F_{T}$ because Block A is being pulled up the incline by the string which is attached to it.

choices.label: D
choices.text: $F_{1}\ =\ F_{T}$ because the string between the blocks is pulling Block B down the incline.

questions.stem: An Atwood's machine consists of two blocks attached to a string that passes over a pulley, as shown. Block A and Block B have masses of $\mathrm{m}_{A}$ and $\mathrm{m}_{B}$ respectively, where $\mathrm{m}_{A}\ <\ \mathrm{m}_{B}$. The masses of the string and pulley are negligible, and the pulley can rotate with negligible friction around its axle. A student draws a free body diagram for each block, as shown. Which of the following is a correct statement regarding the accuracy of the free-body diagrams?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The diagrams are accurate because the force of the string is less than the force of gravity on both blocks.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The diagrams are accurate because the string is pulling up with the same force on both blocks and the gravitational force is greater for Block B.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The diagrams are not accurate because the string will pull up with more force on Block A than Block B since block A has a smaller mass.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The diagrams are not accurate because the gravitational force is independent of mass and will be the same on both blocks. \includegraphics[width=0.47\linewidth]{media/u2_22_q4_38.png}

questions.stem: A box slides up a short, inclined ramp and continues to travel beyond the ramp. Friction and air resistance are negligible. Point $1$ is located on the ramp and Point $2$ is located at the maximum height of the box's path, as shown. Which of the following best represents the free-body diagrams of the block at each location?

A toy car pushes two identical blocks, Block A and Block B, up an inclined ramp at a constant velocity, as shown. The force of friction between the incline and the blocks is negligible. Which of the following pairs of free-body diagrams best represent the free-body diagrams for Block A and Block B?

A large box of mass $M$ is at rest on a platform of mass $\mathrm{m}$, where $M > \mathrm{m}$. These objects are suspended by two strings and each string passes over a separate pulley attached to the ceiling, as shown. Which of the following correctly states the number of upward forces acting on the box-platform system and provides the correct justification?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Two upward forces are exerted on the system because there are two strings which exert upward forces on the system.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Two upward forces are exerted on the system because there are two pulleys which exert upward forces on the system.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Four upward forces are exerted on the system because there are two strings and two pulleys which exert upward forces on the system.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Four upward forces are exerted on the system because there are four tensions which exert upward forces on the system.

questions.stem: A student pushes a box across a rough horizontal surface. Which of the following includes all the forces exerted on the box that are a result of interatomic electric forces?

choices.label: B
choices.text: The force of friction and the normal force

In Figure $1,$ one spring is attached to the end of the other spring. The block is then attached to the end of the bottom spring and set into vertical oscillation of period $T_{1}$. In Figure $2,$ the springs are hung side by side. The block is attached to the bottom ends of both springs and again set into vertical oscillation of period $T_{2}$. What is the ratio $T_{2}/T_{1}$?

A small ball is hung from a string of length $3\ \mathrm{L}_{0}$, as shown in the figures. There is a small peg just to the left of the string at a distance $\mathrm{L}_{0}$ above the center of the ball. The ball is displaced to the left and released from rest, as shown in the middle figure, and moves as a pendulum of length $\mathrm{L}_{0}$ until the string is vertical and loses contact with the peg. The ball then continues moving to the right as a pendulum of length $3\ \mathrm{L}_{0}$, as shown in the right-hand figure, until the string becomes vertical and again contacts the peg. The ball continues moving to the left, again as a pendulum of length $\mathrm{L}_{0}$, until it returns to its initial release position and completes one oscillation, and then the motion is repeated. What is the period of a complete oscillation for the ball?

Two springs, Spring X and Spring Y, are hung vertically and four different metal cylinders of known mass are attached to the bottom of each spring, one at a time. The oscillation period of each cylinder-spring combination is then determined, and the data are used to make a graph of the square of the period versus the cylinder mass, as shown. How are the spring constants $k_{X}$ and $k_{Y}$ related?

A spring hangs vertically from a fixed support with a block attached to the spring's bottom end. The block- spring system is set into oscillation with period $T_{0}$ and maximum speed $v_{0}$. The procedure is then repeated with a different spring and block. The second spring has four times the spring constant of the original spring, the second block has four times the mass of the original block, and the second block-spring system is set into oscillation with half the amplitude of the original system. How do the period and maximum speed of the second system compare to those of the original system? Period Maximum Speed

An object is oscillating in simple harmonic motion. The graph shows the object's velocity as a function of time, with five points on the graph indicated at the labeled times. At which of the following times is the object both accelerating in the positive direction and farther away from equilibrium than it is at time $t_{0}$?

\includegraphics[width=0.36\linewidth]{media/u7_73_q1_179.png}

A cylinder of mass $\mathrm{m}_{C}$ is attached to the bottom end of a vertical spring, which has its top end fixed in place. The cylinder is held in place with the spring at its unstretched length and then released from rest at time $t\ =\ 0.$ The cylinder falls downward, reaches a minimum height that is a distance $D_{0}$ below its release point, and then reverses direction and moves upward again as it undergoes simple harmonic motion. Which of the following is an expression for the cylinder's displacement from equilibrium as a function of time $t$?

A sphere is attached to a vertical spring and oscillates in simple harmonic motion. The sphere's displacement $x$ from equilibrium is described by the differential equation $d^{2}x dt^{2}\ =\ -C^{1 x},$ where $t$ is the time and $C_{1}$ is a positive constant. In a second setup with a different sphere and a different spring, the oscillation frequency is higher than in the original setup. For the second setup, how is the differential equation describing the motion different, if at all, from that of the first setup?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A different constant greater than $C_{1}$ is used.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A different constant less than $C_{1}$ is used.

choices.label: C
choices.text: An additional constant is added to the right-hand side of the equation.

questions.stem:
A simple pendulum is oscillating in simple harmonic motion, and its angular displacement as a function of time is shown in the graph. Which of the following statements about the angular speed and the magnitude of the angular acceleration of the pendulum is correct?

\includegraphics[width=0.38\linewidth]{media/u7_73_q4_180.png}

choices.label: A
choices.text: The angular speed is a maximum at $1\ \mathrm{s}$ and $3\ \mathrm{s}$, and the magnitude of the angular acceleration is a maximum at $0\ \mathrm{s}$, $2\ \mathrm{s}$, and $4\ \mathrm{s}$.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The angular speed is a maximum at $0\ \mathrm{s}$, $2\ \mathrm{s}$, and $4\ \mathrm{s}$, and the magnitude of the angular acceleration is a maximum at $1\ \mathrm{s}$ and $3\ \mathrm{s}$.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Both the angular speed and the magnitude of the angular acceleration are maximum at $1\ \mathrm{s}$ and $3\ \mathrm{s}$.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Both the angular speed and the magnitude of the angular acceleration are maximum at $0\ \mathrm{s}$, $2\ \mathrm{s}$, and $4\ \mathrm{s}$.

questions.stem: A block on a horizontal surface is connected to a horizontal spring, and the other end of the spring is fixed in place. The block is oscillating to the left and to the right as it moves with negligible friction on the surface. The velocity of the block as a function of time is $v(t) =\ v_{max} \cos(\omega t)$, where $v_{max}$ is a positive constant and the positive direction is taken to be to the right. Which of the following correctly describes both the position and the direction of velocity of the block at time $t = \pi/\omega$?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The block is passing through the equilibrium position while moving to the left.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The block is passing through the equilibrium position while moving to the right.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The block is at its maximum displacement to the left of the equilibrium position. It is instantaneously at rest, so there is no direction for the velocity.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The block is at its maximum displacement to the right of the equilibrium position. It is instantaneously at rest, so there is no direction for the velocity. \includegraphics[width=0.4\linewidth]{media/u7_73_q6_181.png}

questions.stem: An object undergoes simple harmonic motion. The graph shows the acceleration of the object as a function of time, and at time $t_{0}$ the acceleration is in the positive direction as indicated. Which of the following describes the object's displacement and velocity at time $t_{0}$?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The object's displacement from equilibrium and its velocity are both in the positive direction.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The object's displacement from equilibrium and its velocity are both in the negative direction.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The object's displacement from equilibrium is in the positive direction, and its velocity is in the negative direction.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The object's displacement from equilibrium is in the negative direction, and its velocity is in the positive direction. \includegraphics[width=0.39\linewidth]{media/u7_73_q7_182.png}

questions.stem: The graph shows the position $x$ as a function of time $t$ for an object in one-dimensional simple harmonic motion. Which of the following expressions gives the object's velocity as a function of $t$?
A block is attached to the bottom of a vertical spring and oscillates with a frequency $f_{0}$ and a maximum acceleration of magnitude a$_{0}$. What is the block's maximum speed?

The figures show a horizontal spring, a horizontal surface, and two identical blocks, Block $1$ and Block $2.$ Initially, as shown in Figure $1,$ only Block $1$ is attached to the spring and oscillates in simple harmonic motion while Block $2$ is held above the surface. At a later time shown in Figure $2,$ Block $1$ is instantaneously at rest and Block $2$ is dropped onto Block $1$ from above. The blocks then move together without slipping, as shown in Figure $3.$ There is negligible friction between Block $1$ and the surface. If the original amplitude and maximum speed of Block 1's motion are A$_{1}$ and $v_{max,1}$ , respectively, what are the amplitude and maximum speed for the two-block system's motion after Block $2$ has been dropped onto Block 1? Amplitude Maximum Speed

A block on a horizontal surface is attached to one end of a horizontal spring, and the other end of the spring is fixed in place. The block is free to move in the $x$-direction along the surface with negligible friction. The block is held in place with the spring stretched some distance from its relaxed length, at which point the block-spring system has a potential energy of $60\ \mathrm{J}$. The block is then released and starts oscillating. If the oscillation period is $1.20$ seconds, how much kinetic energy does the block have $0.20$ seconds after being released?

A block on a horizontal surface is attached to one end of a horizontal spring, and the other end of the spring is fixed in place. The block, which is free to move in the $x$-direction along the surface with negligible friction, oscillates in simple harmonic motion. The block's mass is $2.0\ \mathrm{kg}$, and its motion has an oscillation period of $2.0\ \mathrm{s}$. When the block is $0.30\ \mathrm{m}$ from the equilibrium position, it has a speed of $0.50\ \mathrm{m/s}.$ What is the amplitude of the block's motion?

A block of mass $M_{1}$ is on a horizontal surface and attached to one end of a spring, while the other end of the spring is fixed in place. The block oscillates on the spring with an amplitude A$_{1}$ as it moves with negligible friction on the horizontal surface, and the block-spring system has total mechanical energy $E_{1}$ and maximum kinetic energy $K_{1}$. The block is replaced with a second block that has mass $M_{1}$/2, and the second block is then made to oscillate on the same spring with an amplitude $2$A$_{1}$ . What are the total mechanical energy and maximum kinetic energy of the second block-spring system? Total Mechanical Energy Maximum Kinetic Energy

An object of known mass oscillates horizontally on a spring of known spring constant in simple harmonic motion. At a particular instant the object's kinetic energy $K_{O}$ and the spring's potential energy $U_{S}$ are determined and are both greater than zero, with $U_{S}$ greater than $K_{O}$ . Could the object's distance from equilibrium be equal to the amplitude of oscillation at this instant? What reasoning can be used to support the claim?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Yes. The total mechanical energy of the object-spring system can be calculated by adding $K_{O}$ and $U_{S}$.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes. Most of the system's total mechanical energy is in the form of potential energy, which is true whenever the object's distance from equilibrium is a maximum.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No. The system still has kinetic energy that must be completely converted to potential energy when the object's distance from equilibrium is a maximum.

choices.label: D
choices.text: No. When the kinetic energy is less than half of the system's total mechanical energy, the object is approaching the equilibrium position.

questions.stem: Two identical blocks and two identical springs are arranged in separate block-spring systems, as shown in the figures. In System H, the arrangement is horizontal and the block moves with negligible friction on a horizontal surface. In System V, the arrangement is vertical. The blocks in both systems are set up to oscillate with the same amplitude in simple harmonic motion. Is the maximum energy stored in the spring the same for both systems? What reasoning can be used to support the claim?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Yes. The amplitude of the oscillations is the same for both systems.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes. The two blocks have the same maximum speed.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No. The two springs are different lengths when each system is at equilibrium.

choices.label: D
choices.text: No. The period of oscillation is different for the two systems. \includegraphics[width=0.42\linewidth]{media/u7_74_q6_183.png}

questions.stem: A $2.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ block attached to a horizontal spring oscillates in simple harmonic motion in the horizontal direction. Friction is negligible, so the spring exerts the only horizontal force on the block. The graph shows the spring's potential energy $U$ as a function of the block's position $x$. The block's motion may or may not include positions outside the range shown in the graph. The speed of the block is $3.0\ \mathrm{m/s}$ when the block is at $x\ =\ 0.70\ \mathrm{m}$. At which of the following positions is the speed of the block most nearly equal to $4.0\ \mathrm{m/s}?$

A small rock moves vertically inside a tunnel through a spherical moon that has a uniform density and no atmosphere, as shown in the figure. Inside the tunnel the gravitational force on the rock is proportional to its distance from the moon's center, and the rock undergoes simple harmonic motion after being released from rest at the moon's surface. The rock's kinetic energy is $K_{C}$ when it is passing through the center of the moon. When the rock's kinetic energy is $2\ K_{C}/3,$ is the rock closer to the surface or closer to the center of the moon? What evidence supports the claim?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is closer to the surface. The gravitational force on the rock is a maximum at the surface.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is closer to the surface. The potential energy of the rock-moon system is proportional to the square of the rock's distance from the center.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is closer to the center. The kinetic energy of the rock is more than half of the total mechanical energy of the rock-moon system.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is closer to the center. The gravitational force on the rock is inversely proportional to the square of the distance from the center.

questions.stem: Two identical blocks are each attached to the bottom end of different ideal springs, X and Y. The top ends of these springs are fixed in place. Each block is held in place with each spring at its relaxed length, and the blocks are then released from rest and oscillate vertically. If the spring constant of Spring Y is twice that of Spring X, what is the maximum speed of the block hanging from Spring Y in terms of the maximum speed $v_{max,X}$ of the block hanging from Spring X?

A simple pendulum has a length of $1.0\ \mathrm{m}$ and takes a time $T_{0}$ to complete one oscillation on Earth. What length would a pendulum have to have on Mars, where the acceleration due to gravity is $3.7\ \mathrm{m/s}^{2}$, in order to have the same period?

A physical pendulum is made from a uniform bar with a pivot at its top end. A second physical pendulum is made from another uniform bar of twice the length, also with a pivot at its top end. How does the small- angle oscillation period of the second pendulum compare to that of the first? The rotational inertia about one end for a bar of mass $M$ and length $\mathrm{L}$ is $ML^{2}/3.$

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is less, but more than half as much.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is greater, but less than twice as much.

questions.stem: A physical pendulum is constructed from a hollow hoop, a small sphere, and a rod of negligible mass, as shown in the figure. The small sphere has mass $5\ M_{0}$ and is attached to the top of the hoop, which has mass $M_{0}$ and radius $R_{0}\ =\ 0.080\ \mathrm{m}$. The rod has length $R_{0}/2$ and connects the hoop-sphere system to a pivot about which the pendulum can rotate. What is the period of small-angle oscillations for the pendulum?

A physical pendulum is made from two small spheres attached to a stiff wire of negligible mass and length $\mathrm{L}_{0}$, as shown in the figure. One sphere has mass $M_{0}$ and is at the bottom end of the wire, and the other sphere has mass $2\ M_{0}$ and is at the midpoint of the wire. If the pendulum makes small-angle oscillations, which of the following differential equations describes the pendulum's motion? The pendulum angle $\theta$ is taken relative to the vertical.
A thin hoop undergoes small-angle oscillations about a pivot at its top edge, as shown in the figure. If the oscillation period is $0.70\ \mathrm{s}$, what is the radius of the hoop?

A torsion pendulum consists of a vertical wire connected to a uniform disk of mass $\mathrm{m}_{D}$, radius $r_{D}$, and $2\ /2,$ as shown in the figure. An applied force of magnitude $F_{0}$ is applied tangentially rotational inertia $\mathrm{m}_{D}r_{D}$ to the disk, holding it in place at an angular displacement $\theta_{max}$ from the wire's relaxed angular position. The applied force is then removed, and the disk undergoes rotational simple harmonic motion. What is the angular acceleration of the disk when its angular displacement from equilibrium is $\theta_{max}/2?$

A uniform rod of length $\mathrm{L}_{R}$ and mass $M_{R}$ is free to rotate about a pivot located a distance $\ell$, where $\ell \ll \mathrm{L}_{R}$, above the rod's center, as shown in the figure. Which of the following changes could result in a shorter $2 /12.$ period for small-angle oscillations of the rod? The rotational inertia about the center of the rod is $M_{R}\mathrm{L}_{R}$

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increasing the mass of the rod to $2\ M_{R}$.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Decreasing the mass of the rod to $M_{R}/2.$ \includegraphics[width=0.15\linewidth]{media/u7_75_q7_186.png}

The planet has $1/40$ the mass and $1/5$ the radius of Earth. The bar has mass $M_{0}$ and rotational inertia $I_{0}\ =\ M_{0}\mathrm{L}_{0} ^{2}/3 about$ the pivot axis. Which of the following differential equations describes the pendulum's motion, where $\mathrm{g}$ is the acceleration of gravity on Earth?
